mappings.note: That the seal symbols amount to a writing system is one of the defining marks of the first cities on the Indus. Not LO-109, since the item claims a civilisational achievement rather than reading the seals as evidence.
Citadel on raised ground against the lower town - a town-planning contrast within the first cities, so LO-113.
Matches artefacts to their materials and settles on the bronze Dancing Girl: artefact knowledge (LO-109) plus the metal-working skill LO-124 covers.
Warehouses as stores for surplus and trade goods - civic architecture of the first cities, hence LO-113 rather than the external-trade outcome.
'Elite' as the ruling or administrative group living apart in the citadel; social organisation inside the first cities. Not LO-116, whose diversity is the pupil's own society.
Rejects the Aryan-invasion claim among statements on cotton, drainage and climate - all facts about the Indus cities and their decline.
Turns on Harappans EXPORTING carnelian rather than importing it (LO-123) and on Lothal's basin being a dockyard (LO-110).
Identifies small carved steatite objects as seals from their material, motifs and find context - pure artefact interpretation, so LO-109.
The Priest King as a symbolic artefact whose identity is uncertain; a statement about what an excavated object can and cannot tell us, which is LO-109.
Uniform build quality across large and small houses read as standardised practice - a town-planning inference about the first cities.
Rules out 'Vedic' from the names of the earliest civilisation, which requires knowing that the Vedic period came later; a chronological fact about the Indus cities.
Cotton cultivation giving woven cloth in place of skins - an advance of the Indus civilisation over earlier peoples, so LO-113. The 'first in Eurasia' version of this item also draws in LO-124.
Reads hypothetical irrigation canals as evidence of deliberate water management: an inference from excavated features (LO-109) about Harappan farming (LO-113).
Separates the animals the Harappans domesticated from the lion they only depicted - a fact about their husbandry, under LO-113.
The turn to rural settlement after the cities failed; the closing phase of the first-cities development.
That crafts and traditions outlived the cities is a claim about continuity across periods, which is the synthesis LO-115 asks for, resting on the Indus development itself.
The 73-metre reservoir at Dholavira - a measurement of the cities' water engineering, so LO-113 rather than LO-110, which is for placing the site.
Defines pulses as the legume seeds the Harappans grew; part of their agricultural base under LO-113.
Names 'civilisation' as the stage marked by government and urbanism - the concept behind the first-cities development.
Asks for one defining feature of a civilisation - government, urbanism, crafts, trade or writing; the same conceptual ground as the definition item.

Defines metallurgy as extracting, purifying and alloying metals - precisely the 'knowledge of metals' that LO-124 lists among India's contributions. Not LO-113, which covers the cities rather than the craft knowledge.
Mesopotamia as the first region to reach civilisation; LO-113's clause about relating developments in one place with another covers the comparison.
The start date of about 2600 BCE for the Indus-Sarasvati cities; a plain fact about the first-cities development.
Harappa as the first site excavated - about the archaeological work itself, so LO-109, as with the 1920s multiple-choice version.
'First Urbanisation' as the label for this development - the same phrase LO-113 is built to cover.
Defines a tributary. That is river vocabulary, which sits with India's physical features in LO-107 rather than with the Indus cities.
The Sarasvati's modern name, Ghaggar - identifying an Indian river on the ground today, so LO-107. Not LO-111, which is for what the Rig Veda says about it.
Which ancient text first praises the Sarasvati: the Rig Veda. A question about the contents of a literary work of the time, hence LO-111.
Bricks as the standard building material of Harappan cities - the short-answer twin of the baked-bricks multiple choice.
Names the protective city wall a fortification; urban vocabulary of the first cities.
Names the Great Bath from its dimensions. The city is given in the stem, so nothing has to be located and LO-110 does not apply; the demand is knowledge of the structure.
Defines a reservoir - the water-storage vocabulary of the Harappan cities, with the fortification item.
Names a Harappan cereal such as barley or wheat; their farming base under LO-113.

The Harappans as the FIRST in Eurasia to grow cotton - both a fact about the Indus cities (LO-113) and a genuine Indian first that LO-124's contributions clause covers. The plain cotton-and-clothing item takes LO-113 alone.
The Banawali plough model: an artefact (LO-109) evidencing Harappan tillage (LO-113), mapped like its multiple-choice twin.
Names carnelian as the Harappan bead stone - a craft material of the Indus cities, kept off LO-124, which is used here for metals.
Bronze as copper alloyed with tin; the alloying knowledge that LO-124 names explicitly, so it goes with the metallurgy definition rather than with the city items.
Names Lothal as the Gujarat site with the dockyard basin - a site-identification item, so LO-110.
Names the small square animal-and-script objects as seals; artefact vocabulary, so LO-109.
Steatite as the stone the seals were cut from before firing - another fact about the artefacts themselves, under LO-109.
